common_name: Lady Di Bower Vine (White Bower of Beauty)
directions: Lady Di is a pure-white-flowered selection of Bower Vine that lacks the rose-pink throat markings typical of the species, showing instead a faint pale-yellow blush deep in the flower tube for a cleaner, all-white floral display. It shares the species' vigorous twining habit and fine, glossy, pinnately-compound foliage, blooming heaviest in spring with scattered flowers through the warm months. Because seedlings will not reliably reproduce the pure white color, plants are propagated from stem cuttings rather than seed. Grow it as you would the species, in full sun to partial shade on well-drained soil, with afternoon shade appreciated during peak summer heat.

common_name: Rosea Bower Vine (Pink Bower of Beauty)
directions: Rosea is the classic deep-pink-flowered selection of Bower Vine, bearing clusters of funnel-shaped flowers in soft rose-pink with a darker rose-red throat, a more moderate-sized bloom than the larger 'Rosea Superba' selection. The vine keeps the species' fine-textured, airy, evergreen foliage and twining growth habit, making it a dependable cover for arbors, fences, and pergolas in zone 9-11 gardens. It flowers most heavily in spring with intermittent rebloom through the warm season and tolerates brief cold dips better than many other tropical flowering vines. Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade and prune lightly after the main spring flush to maintain shape.

Charisma is grown chiefly for its ornamental foliage, each leaflet edged in creamy white against a deep green center, giving the vine year-round visual interest even outside the bloom season. It still produces the species' funnel-shaped, softly fragrant pink flowers with a rose-red throat, though somewhat less densely than green-leaved forms, and it tends to be a more restrained, compact grower. Give it bright light to keep the cream variegation from fading to plain green, along with the same well-drained soil and moderate watering recommended for the species. Propagate from cuttings to maintain the variegated leaf pattern true to type.

Golden Showers is a yellow-flowered selection of the Wonga Wonga Vine, replacing the creamy, maroon-throated blooms of the wild species with a profuse display of clear golden-yellow tubular flowers in late winter and spring. It keeps the species' dense, twining growth habit and glossy, fine-textured evergreen foliage, climbing readily on wire or trellis and tolerating both coastal exposure and drier inland sites once established. Prune after the main spring bloom to control size and encourage compact, floriferous new growth. Grow in well-drained soil, since prolonged waterlogging stresses the root system.

Clerodendrum inerme, commonly called Seaside Clerodendrum or Sorcerer's Bush, is a dense, rounded evergreen shrub native to coastal areas from East Africa through tropical Asia and northern Australia, prized above all for its exceptional tolerance of salt spray, salty soil, and strong coastal wind. It bears small white tubular flowers with slender, protruding purple-red stamens held just above the glossy foliage, flowering intermittently through the warm season and followed by small dark berry-like fruit. Because it tolerates heavy shearing, it is widely grown as a clipped hedge, screen, or topiary specimen in coastal landscapes, and can also be trained into a small single-trunk tree form. Give it full sun to light shade and well-drained soil; once established it is markedly drought- and salt-tolerant and needs only occasional supplemental water.

Lolly Bush is a small evergreen tree or large shrub native to monsoonal and coastal regions of northern Australia, grown both as a screening or specimen plant and for its ripe fruit, which gives off a distinctive sweet, confectionery-like fragrance that inspired the common name. In spring and summer it produces clusters of small, fragrant, pale pink to white flowers followed by shiny black fruit set against persistent red-orange calyces, creating an attractive two-toned display that draws fruit-eating birds. It tolerates a wide range of soils from sandy loam to heavier clay and, once established, handles extended dry spells typical of its native monsoon climate. Grow in full sun to light shade; it responds well to pruning for a denser hedge form or can be left to develop its natural small-tree habit.

This slender, rosemary-leaved rockrose forms a wiry, upright mound of narrow dark-green foliage that releases a resinous scent in hot weather, typical of the limestone matorral of southeastern Spain and the Balearics. White, papery flowers barely an inch across open for a single day each but succeed one another in flushes from mid-spring onward. It demands the leanest, best-drained soil available and resents any summer irrigation once rooted in, making it a good match for gravel gardens and rocky banks. Skip feeding and avoid cutting back into bare wood, since old Cistus growth rarely resprouts.

Native to the siliceous matorral and open woodland margins of central and western Iberia, this is one of the taller, more upright rockroses, with broad, crinkled, heart-shaped leaves that resemble a small poplar leaf rather than the narrow foliage typical of the genus. Clear white flowers with a yellow center open in generous flushes through late spring and early summer against the rich green foliage. It tolerates slightly more organic soil than many Cistus but still fails in poorly drained or heavily irrigated ground. Prune lightly right after flowering to maintain a dense habit, never into leafless wood.

This rounded, densely branched broom is a characteristic member of the western Mediterranean matorral of Spain, Portugal, and northwest Africa, holding tight clusters of small, bright-yellow pea flowers near the branch tips in spring on an otherwise spiny, almost leafless silhouette. Its tolerance of shallow, stony, nutrient-poor soils that defeat most garden shrubs makes it valuable for dry banks and scree plantings. Like other brooms it dislikes root disturbance and rich feeding, which produces lanky, short-lived growth instead of the tight, wiry habit it shows in the wild. Established plants need no irrigation beyond natural rainfall in a Mediterranean-type climate.

Retama is a wide, fountain-shaped shrub of the dry steppes and matorral of central and southern Spain and Portugal, built almost entirely of slender, rush-like, blue-green stems that photosynthesize in place of its scant, short-lived leaves. Masses of small, fragrant, white-and-yellow pea flowers smother the weeping branches in spring, drawing heavy bee activity. Its extraordinarily deep root system lets it tap moisture far below the surface, giving it exceptional drought tolerance once past its first year or two. Use it as an airy, low-water specimen or informal screen in Mediterranean and desert-climate gardens, and avoid summer irrigation once mature.

Native to exposed limestone matorral and rocky slopes of the Iberian and Moroccan high mountains, hedgehog broom forms a dense, intensely spiny dome built of rigid, interlacing spines rather than conventional leaves. Small, fragrant, violet-blue pea flowers stud the whole cushion in late spring, giving a striking contrast against the grey-green spine mass. It is a favorite of alpine and rock-garden growers for its sculptural, almost sea-urchin-like form and genuine cold hardiness, well beyond what its Mediterranean origin might suggest, provided drainage is sharp and winter wet is avoided. Grow in a scree bed, trough, or raised bed with gritty, lean, alkaline soil and full sun.

Endemic to the sandy and schist matorral of Portugal and western Spain, this lavender is immediately distinctive for its unusually long, threadlike purple-black bracts that dangle well below the compact flower spike, far more exaggerated than the short bracts of the related Lavandula stoechas. The grey, finely cut foliage carries a sharper, more resinous, camphor-like scent than English lavender. It needs the same lean, gritty, fast-draining soil and hot, sunny exposure as its Mediterranean relatives, and resents both winter wet and rich feeding. Give it a light trim after flowering to keep the mound compact, avoiding cuts into old bare wood.

This slender bulb of the stony matorral and olive-grove margins of Portugal and western Spain produces a single wiry stem topped by one to several nodding, bell-shaped flowers in muted bronze, maroon, and dull yellow tones, often faintly checkered. It is a plant of the specialist bulb trade, prized for an understated, almost somber beauty rather than bold color. Grow it in a bulb frame, raised bed, or dry sunny border where summer baking and sharp winter drainage mimic its native dry-summer climate, and let the foliage die back fully before the bulb's dormant season. It increases slowly by offsets and resents disturbance once settled.

A diminutive relative of the bearded iris found scattered through grassy matorral and open scrub across Iberia and the wider Mediterranean, this corm sends up a few grass-like leaves and short-lived, pale violet-blue, iris-like flowers that open only in the afternoon and typically fade by the following morning. Each flower lasts barely a day, but a single corm produces a succession of blooms over several weeks in spring. It needs a hot, dry summer dormancy to flower reliably, making it best suited to a bulb frame, raised bed, or gritty Mediterranean-style border rather than a regularly irrigated bed. Corms multiply slowly and can be lifted and divided once the foliage yellows.

A conspicuous and long-lived feature of Iberian and wider Mediterranean matorral and garrigue, this tuberous-rooted perennial sends up a rosette of strap-shaped leaves followed by tall, branched flower spikes crowded with star-shaped white flowers marked with a brown midrib, opening in succession from late winter into spring. Its thick, fleshy root tubers store water and nutrients, letting the plant persist through the harshest summer drought and resprout reliably from the same clump for decades. It needs full sun and sharp drainage and is best left undisturbed once planted. After flowering the foliage dies back for a long dry-season dormancy, so pair it with companions that fill the summer gap.

subcategory: mallee eucalyptus grown for oil and ornament
directions: Blue mallee grows as a multi-stemmed, lignotuber-forming small tree in the mallee woodlands of Victoria and New South Wales, its narrow blue-green leaves carrying an exceptionally high concentration of cineole-rich oil that makes it the principal species grown for commercial eucalyptus oil distillation in Australia. The smooth, often mottled grey-brown bark and open, multi-trunked habit give it strong ornamental structure even without flowers. It thrives on shallow, infertile mallee soils and tolerates both drought and moderate frost once established, resprouting readily from its woody rootstock if coppiced or burned back. Give it full sun and sharp drainage, and avoid rich, regularly irrigated soils that encourage soft, short-lived growth.

One of the most widespread multi-stemmed mallees of semi-arid southern Australia, this species forms dense stands of slender grey-barked trunks rising from a single underground lignotuber, with narrow grey-green leaves and small cream flower clusters in late spring to summer. Its tough, smooth-to-fibrous bark and extreme drought tolerance reflect an origin in the low, erratic rainfall of inland mallee country. In cultivation it is used mainly for revegetation, windbreaks, and dry-garden screening rather than as a specimen tree. Give it full sun and fast drainage, and expect it to resprout readily from the lignotuber if top growth is damaged.

White mallee, also called congoo mallee, is a classic multi-trunked, lignotuber-forming eucalyptus of the mallee woodlands spanning Victoria, New South Wales, and South Australia, with smooth whitish to grey bark shedding in ribbons and small white summer flower clusters that draw native bees. It occupies some of the most nutrient-poor, calcareous mallee soils in its range and survives long dry spells by drawing on reserves stored in its large underground lignotuber. In gardens it works best as a dry-climate screen, windbreak, or habitat planting rather than a feature tree. Plant in full sun with sharp drainage and avoid supplemental summer watering once roots are established.

Ridge-fruited mallee is a shrubby, multi-stemmed eucalyptus of sandy mallee woodland and dune scrub across southern Australia, grown in native-plant horticulture chiefly for its showy flowers, large pink to red blossoms with prominent stamens that open from distinctively ribbed, urn-shaped buds in late winter and spring. Thick, leathery, glaucous-blue-green leaves and smooth grey bark add further ornamental interest to its naturally gnarled, wind-shaped form. It needs deep, sharply drained sandy soil and full sun, performing poorly in heavy clay or regularly irrigated ground. Once established it is extremely drought-hardy and well suited to a dry-garden feature planting.

This long-lived, spiny hummock grass is the dominant understory species of mallee woodland across semi-arid southern Australia, forming a dense, domed tussock of rigid, needle-sharp, resin-coated leaves that can persist and slowly expand outward for a century or more without replanting. It is adapted to deep infertile sand and relies on an intact, undisturbed root system, making nursery tubestock far more reliable than attempts at division or seed in cultivation. In a dry garden it provides an authentic textural anchor for a mallee-themed planting alongside eucalypts and saltbush, but its sharp foliage calls for placement away from paths. Give it full sun, sharp drainage, and no summer irrigation once established.

subcategory: mallee and chenopod shrubland understory shrub
directions: Pearl bluebush is a rounded, densely branched chenopod shrub that forms a major understory component of mallee woodland and chenopod shrubland across inland South Australia and adjoining regions, prized in cultivation for its fine, pearly-silver, cylindrical leaves that give the whole plant a soft, frosted appearance. It is extremely tolerant of drought, grazing, and saline or calcareous soils that few ornamentals will grow in. Use it as a textural contrast shrub in a dry-garden or mallee-themed border alongside eucalypts and saltbush. Plant in full sun with sharp drainage and avoid rich, moisture-retentive soils that shorten its lifespan.

Spiny saltbush is a sprawling, wide understory shrub common beneath mallee eucalypts and in open scrub across semi-arid southern Australia, its small, fleshy, silver-grey leaves and sparsely spine-tipped branches forming loose, low mounds that knit together bare ground between larger shrubs. Small red to purple berries follow the inconspicuous flowers and are eaten by birds. It tolerates saline, calcareous, and nutrient-poor soils and extended drought, making it valuable for erosion control and informal groundcover beneath a mallee-themed planting. Grow in full sun with sharp drainage and minimal supplemental water once established.

Silver turkey bush is an upright, fine-textured emu bush of mallee and arid shrubland across inland Australia, its narrow, silver-grey, resinous foliage giving a soft, shimmering haze that contrasts well against darker eucalypt and saltbush companions. Small, pale mauve to lilac tubular flowers appear mainly in winter and spring, offering a modest nectar source for honeyeaters. Like most Eremophila it demands sharp drainage and minimal summer moisture, rotting quickly in heavy or frequently irrigated soils, and is best grown from cuttings of selected forms rather than seed. Use it as a background or screening shrub in a dry mallee-style garden, in full sun on lean soil.

Moonah is a gnarled, dense-crowned small tree or large shrub found both as a mallee woodland associate on inland calcareous soils and as a dominant coastal species across southern Australia, with fine, needle-like grey-green leaves and small cream bottlebrush flower spikes in late summer. Its twisted, weathered trunk and rough, fibrous papery bark give it strong sculptural character even without bloom. It tolerates salt spray, wind, drought, and poor calcareous soils that defeat most trees, making it a durable windbreak or screening choice for difficult dry sites. Plant in full sun with good drainage and expect slow but very long-lived growth once established.

Rhodoleia championii is a slow-growing evergreen shrub or small tree from the hillside forests of Hong Kong and southern China, prized for its nodding clusters of waxy, rose-pink flowers that open in late winter when little else is in bloom. Plant it in dappled or partial shade with acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil, ideally sheltered from harsh winter wind and prolonged freezes. Young plants benefit from the protection of overhead tree canopy, while established specimens tolerate brief dips into the low 20s F and modest drought once their roots are settled. Its leathery, dark green foliage and architectural branching make it a handsome specimen for a woodland garden long after the flowers fade.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — Plants of the World Online
Hong Kong Herbarium / Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department

directions: Chimonanthus praecox 'Grandiflorus' is a selection of Chinese wintersweet valued for flowers noticeably larger than the species, with butter-yellow outer petals surrounding a deep maroon-purple throat, opening on bare stems during the coldest weeks of winter. The spicy, citrus-and-jasmine fragrance carries well beyond the plant, making it a favorite near paths and doorways. Site it in part shade or morning sun with its roots shaded and its crown reaching toward light, in fertile, well-drained soil, since it dislikes waterlogged ground. Prune immediately after flowering to maintain shape, since buds for the following winter form on the current season's growth.
sources: Dirr, M.A. — Manual of Woody Landscape Plants

directions: Chimonanthus praecox 'Luteus' bears flowers of a clear, uniform wax-yellow with none of the purplish staining found at the center of the common species, giving the winter display a cleaner, brighter look against bare branches. It typically opens its richly fragrant flowers a bit later in the season than the species or 'Grandiflorus,' helping stretch the wintersweet display further into late winter. Grow it in partial shade to ease the stress of hot afternoon sun, in moisture-retentive but well-drained, fertile soil. Like other wintersweets, it flowers best with some protection from harsh winter wind.

Eleutherococcus sieboldianus 'Variegatus' is a twiggy, arching deciduous shrub from China grown for its palmately compound leaves, each leaflet edged in a crisp white margin that brightens shaded corners of the garden from spring through fall. Few variegated shrubs perform as reliably in deep shade, making this an especially useful plant for difficult north-facing foundations or plantings beneath dense tree canopy. It tolerates poor soil, urban pollution, and some drought once established, and responds well to renewal pruning to control its suckering, thicket-forming habit. Inconspicuous greenish flowers appear in early summer and are followed by small black berries, but the foliage remains the main attraction.
sources: Dirr, M.A. — Manual of Woody Landscape Plants

directions: Platycarya is a distinctive East Asian relative of walnut and hickory, grown for its upright, persistent fruiting catkins that look like small woody pine cones, formed from densely overlapping winged nutlets rather than true cone scales. Its pinnately compound leaves and overall habit resemble a small hickory, and mature trees develop a rounded crown with attractive gray-brown bark. Site it in well-drained, fertile soil with full sun to light shade and protect young trees from prolonged drought until established. It remains uncommon in cultivation outside botanical collections, but the curious cone-like fruit clusters make it a worthwhile specimen tree for collectors of unusual nut-bearing hardwoods.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (Bean's Trees and Shrubs)

directions: Japanese wingnut is a fast-growing mountain forest tree from Japan, closely related to Caucasian wingnut but distinguished by leaflets that attach directly to an unwinged leaf rachis. Clusters of small winged nutlets dangle from long pendulous strings through summer, giving the tree an airy, tassel-hung appearance. It thrives in deep, moisture-retentive soil along streambanks and tolerates occasional flooding far better than most large shade trees, though it is less commonly offered than its Caucasian cousin. Reserve it for parkland, arboreta, or spacious sites, since mature trees can exceed seventy feet with a broad, rounded crown and a tendency to sucker.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (Bean's Trees and Shrubs)
Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew - Plants of the World Online

directions: Bitter cherry is a thicket-forming wild cherry native from British Columbia south through the Rockies and Sierra Nevada into California, often colonizing disturbed ground, burned sites, and forest edges. Clusters of small white flowers open in spring before or with the leaves, followed by small red-to-nearly-black drupes that are intensely bitter to people but heavily used by songbirds, grouse, and bears. Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; established plants are drought-tolerant and need little care, spreading by root suckers to form dense wildlife thickets. It is primarily grown for habitat and erosion-control restoration plantings rather than as an edible fruit crop.

Desert almond is a wiry, spine-tipped shrub of the Mojave, Sonoran, and Great Basin deserts, found on dry washes, rocky slopes, and alluvial fans across California, Nevada, Arizona, and Utah. Small clusters of pale pink to white flowers appear in early spring, followed by tiny, dry, felted fruits enclosing a hard almond-like pit that is too bitter to eat but provides forage for desert rodents and birds. It demands sharply drained, gravelly or sandy soil and essentially no irrigation once rooted, making it valuable for xeriscaping and desert restoration rather than table fruit. Its dense, thorny branching also offers nesting cover for desert birds in otherwise sparse terrain.

Desert apricot is a spiny, drought-adapted shrub restricted to the dry washes and rocky slopes of California's Colorado Desert and adjacent Baja California, where it is often among the first shrubs to flower each year. Fragrant pale yellow blossoms open on bare branches in late winter, well ahead of the leaves, and are an important early nectar source for native bees. The small yellow-orange, apricot-like drupes that follow are thin-fleshed and seedy but are readily eaten by birds and other desert wildlife. Grow it in lean, fast-draining soil in full sun with minimal irrigation.

Chinese raspberry is a vigorous bramble native to eastern China, grown both for its orange-red, raspberry-like aggregate fruit and, in traditional Chinese herbal practice, for the dried unripe fruit known as fu pen zi. Deeply lobed, palmate leaves and arching, lightly prickled canes distinguish it from the more familiar red and black raspberries grown in Western gardens. Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade and train the long canes onto a trellis or fence. It fruits on second-year canes much like traditional raspberries, so prune out spent canes after harvest to keep the planting productive.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew - Plants of the World Online

directions: Sycamore fig is a massive, spreading fig tree native across sub-Saharan Africa, the Nile Valley, and the Arabian Peninsula, historically significant as the biblical sycomore and long valued for shade, timber, and fruit along riverbanks and floodplains. Its figs form in dense hanging clusters directly on the trunk and older branches rather than among the leaves, a growth habit known as cauliflory, and ripen through much of the year in warm climates. Full seed-viable fruiting depends on pollination by a specific fig wasp absent from most cultivated regions outside Africa and the Middle East, so fruit set elsewhere is often sparse or seedless. Give it a large, open planting site in full sun with deep, well-drained soil, since mature trees develop an immense buttressed trunk and wide-spreading canopy unsuited to small gardens.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew - Plants of the World Online
